extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians in discrete / computational geometry and readers verifying a computer-assisted proof
extracted.subtask_description: A complete (abridged) computer-assisted proof of the Kepler conjecture (optimal density of sphere packings in R^3) built by reducing the infinite-dimensional packing problem to a finite-dimensional optimization on a compact space of decomposition stars and eliminating counterexamples by combinatorial classification, linear programming, and branch-and-bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of the Kepler conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 1.1 (The Kepler conjecture). No packing of congruent balls in Euclidean three space has density greater than that of the face-centered cubic packing. This density is π/√18 ≈ 0.74.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem is the target to be proved. All subsequent constructions and reductions are aimed at showing no packing exceeds this density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negligible function
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 1.2. A : Λ → R is negligible if there is a constant C1 such that for all r ≥ 1 and all x ∈ R^3, sum_{v ∈ Λ(x,r)} A(v) ≤ C1 r^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negligibility is a growth-control criterion for corrections A(v) attached to Voronoi cells; it ensures the correction contributes only lower-order terms to density bounds (O(r^2) vs. volume ~ r^3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fcc-compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 1.2. A : Λ → R is fcc-compatible if for all v ∈ Λ we have √32 ≤ vol(Ω(v)) + A(v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the corrected volume vol(Ω(v)) + A(v) is always at least the Voronoi cell volume in the face-centered cubic (fcc) packing. Fcc-compatibility combined with negligibility yields the global density bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density bound from negligible fcc-compatible function
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 1.3. If there exists a negligible fcc-compatible function A : Λ → R for a saturated packing Λ, then there exists a constant C such that for all r ≥ 1 and all x ∈ R^3, δ(x,r,Λ) ≤ π/√18 + C/r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the key analytic implication: constructing a negligible, fcc-compatible correction A suffices to bound asymptotic packing density by π/√18. The proof shows how negligibility and fcc-compatibility control the numerator/denominator in local density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-dimensional reduction via decomposition stars and A0
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 1.5. For each saturated packing Λ and each v ∈ Λ there is a decomposition star D(v,Λ) ∈ DS such that the function A defined by A(v) = A0(D(v,Λ)) is negligible for Λ. Here DS is a compact topological space of decomposition stars and A0 : DS → R is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: reduce the infinite-dimensional problem to a finite-dimensional optimization. The local data around a vertex (decomposition star) determine A(v). One must construct DS, define A0 continuously on DS, and prove the negligibility of the induced A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of the scoring function σ
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition following (1.4). The scoring function σ : DS → R is a continuous function obtained by composing the finite-dimensional version of Inequality (1.3) with a linear function; explicitly σ(D) = −4 δ_oct (vol(Ω(D)) + A0(D)) + 16π/3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing vol(Ω(D)) + A0(D) ≥ √32 for all D ∈ DS is equivalent (via this linear combination) to showing σ(D) ≤ 8 pt for all D. Thus bounding σ on DS is the finite-dimensional optimization problem to solve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum of σ on DS equals 8 pt (finite-dimensional goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 1.7 (Finite dimensional reduction). The maximum of σ on the topological space DS of all decomposition stars is the constant 8 pt ≈ 0.442989.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving this inequality (σ(D) ≤ 8 pt for all D with equality only at fcc/hcp local configurations) is central: it implies fcc-compatibility of A0 and thus, by earlier lemmas, the Kepler conjecture. The proof strategy is to assume a contravening D with σ(D) > 8 pt and eliminate possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contravening decomposition star
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 1.2/1.3 context. D is called contravening if σ(D) ≥ 8 pt (and much of the subsequent reasoning tacitly assumes decomposition stars under discussion are contravening).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A contravening star is a candidate counterexample to σ(D) ≤ 8 pt. The proof proceeds by associating combinatorial data to any contravening star and eliminating those possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association to plane graph and tameness
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1.2/Claim 1.12. To each contravening decomposition star D one associates a combinatorial plane graph G(D). Claim 1.12: The plane graph of a contravening decomposition star is tame (satisfies the restrictive list of properties in Section 7.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This associates a finite combinatorial invariant (a plane graph) to each local geometric configuration. Tameness restricts the class of possible graphs and is essential to reduce the problem to a finite classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of tame plane graphs (finite archival list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim 1.13 / Theorem 8.1. If a plane graph is tame, then it is isomorphic to one of the several thousand plane graphs that appear in the archival list of plane graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By classifying all tame graphs (finite list, stored in the archive), the geometric problem reduces to finitely many combinatorial cases, each of which can be analyzed separately (often by LP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction from archival list to three candidate graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim 1.14. If the plane graph of a contravening decomposition star is isomorphic to one in the archival list, then it is isomorphic to one of the following three plane graphs: Gpent, Ghcp, or Gfcc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrows the possible combinatorial types for contravening stars to just three special graphs; the rest are eliminated by linear-programming/branch-and-bound arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of the pentahedral prism case (Gpent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim 1.15 / Theorem 1.10 (Ferguson). There are no contravening decomposition stars D whose associated plane graph is isomorphic to Gpent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ferguson's thesis establishes that Gpent cannot arise as a contravening configuration; this removes that troublesome combinatorial case from consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local optimality of fcc and hcp (equality cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim 1.16. If D is a contravening decomposition star and the plane graph of D is isomorphic to Gfcc or Ghcp, then σ(D) = 8 pt. Moreover, up to Euclidean motion, U(D) is the kissing arrangement of twelve balls around a central ball in the fcc or hcp packing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the characterization of maxima: the only configurations attaining the σ maximum are the local fcc/hcp kissing arrangements. Establishing local optimality requires careful geometric analysis (Chapter 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and nonoverlap of the Q-system
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 2.8 and Theorem 2.9. The Q-system Q is a canonically associated set of simplices (quasi-regular tetrahedra and strict quarters) defined by a list of inclusion rules; Theorem 2.9: for every saturated packing there exists a uniquely determined Q-system and distinct simplices in the Q-system have disjoint interiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Q-system partitions high-density parts of space into finite simplices amenable to local analysis. Proving its uniqueness and nonoverlap is necessary to control combinatorics and avoid double-counting in scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear programming relaxation and branch-and-bound elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1.4 and Chapters 12–14. Attach a linear program to each tame graph G as a relaxation of the nonlinear optimization over decomposition stars with graph G. If the LP maximum < 8 pt, then no contravening star with graph G exists; otherwise use branch-and-bound, refined LPs, and specialized inequalities to eliminate the remaining cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the principal computational strategy: LP relaxations give rigorous upper bounds (since they relax constraints). Branch-and-bound and case-splitting (face refinements, upright/flat quarter branching, interval-based inequalities) produce tighter bounds until every non-fcc/hcp graph is eliminated. Calculations and logfiles are archived ([Hal05],[Hal06a]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exact numeric constants and truncation parameter
rubrics_metrics.description: Deﬁnition 2.1 and remarks: choose truncation parameter t0 = 1.255 (2t0 = 2.51) and numerous decimal constants used throughout; each decimal constant is an exact rational value (e.g., 2t0 = 251/100) and should be treated as exact, not approximations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All numeric constants used in inequalities, pivots, LP bounds, and computer calculations are exact rational values in the formal arguments; careful bookkeeping of these constants is required for rigorous bounds and reproducible computer verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness and continuity of DS and σ
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 4 / Section summaries. DS (space of decomposition stars) is a compact topological space that embeds into finite-dimensional Euclidean space, and σ : DS → R is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compactness and continuity justify existence of maxima of σ and allow finite-dimensional optimization methods to be applied. The reduction to a finite-variable problem relies on these topological properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational verification and archival resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Section remarks and references: many parts of the proof rely on computer calculations; details and log files are available at Hal05 and the unabridged version Hal06a. Certain constants, penalties, and LP-derived inequalities reference specific computation logs (e.g., calc- numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof is computer-assisted: numerical LP bounds, interval arithmetic, and combinatorial enumeration are used. Reproducibility requires access to archived computations and careful numerical verification consistent with the exact rational constants used in the paper.
